topic: Why do people procrastinate even when they know what they need to do?
audience_pain: People feel stuck between knowing an important task matters and repeatedly choosing tiny distractions, then blaming themselves for the delay.
emotional_angle: Relief before guilt: procrastination is framed with compassion as a short-term escape from discomfort.

hooks.text: You know what to do - so why does starting feel impossible?
The real reason procrastination can feel harder than doing nothing.
hooks.rationale: Creates curiosity around a familiar frustration.

hooks.text: If guilt could make you productive, you would be finished by now.
This is not laziness. It is a short-term relief loop.
Before you call yourself lazy, notice what you are avoiding.
hooks.rationale: Invites self-reflection and promises a useful shift.

selected_hook.text: Before you call yourself lazy, notice what you are avoiding.
selected_hook.rationale: Invites self-reflection and promises a useful shift.

story.summary: A capable person opens an important task, feels a flash of pressure, and reaches for a smaller distraction that offers immediate relief.
beats: A harmless distraction offers instant relief.
The relief fades and guilt arrives.
The next action is made smaller and concrete.
examples: A student opens a blank assignment and starts reorganizing notes instead.
An employee delays one difficult email by clearing easy notifications.
pattern_interrupts: Pause: what feeling appears one second before you switch tasks?
Try this: name the next action in five words.

psychology_insights.claim: Procrastination can function as a way to escape an unpleasant feeling in the moment.
psychology_insights.evidence_or_reasoning: Avoiding a difficult task can quickly reduce discomfort, which can make avoidance more likely the next time similar discomfort appears.
psychology_insights.recommended_wording: One useful way to view procrastination is as short-term emotion management, not simply a failure of planning.

lesson: Do not argue with yourself into action. Shrink the task until the next step feels safe enough to start.
cta: Comment with the one task you will reduce to a two-minute first step today.

final_script: You know what to do - so why does starting feel impossible? Why do people procrastinate even when they know what they need to do? Imagine opening the task, feeling pressure in your chest, then checking one tiny thing on your phone. For a moment, the pressure drops. That relief is the trap: your brain learns that avoiding the task changes the feeling fast. This does not mean you are lazy. It may mean the task feels too vague, too risky, or too loaded. Instead of promising to finish everything, choose the smallest visible move: open the document, write one messy sentence, or set a two-minute timer. Starting is the payoff. Comment with the task you will shrink today.
